# forgesworn/anvil

> Forge-hardened release tool for JS/TS libraries. Multi-runner
> reproducible-build attestation, OIDC trusted publishing, SLSA
> provenance, pre-publish secret scan, exports-map check, frozen-vector
> gate, runtime-only npm audit, action-pin auditing. Pure bash, ~1600
> lines, auditable in thirty minutes.

## What this is

A GitHub Action (reusable workflow + composite fallback) that publishes
npm packages with hard pre-publish gates. Zero dependencies, pure bash,
auditable in thirty minutes.

The flagship feature: two parallel CI builds on independent runners must
produce byte-identical tarballs, or the release is blocked. No other
JS release tool offers this today.

## Who it's for

Any JavaScript/TypeScript library author who publishes to npm and wants
a release pipeline with fewer moving parts than the library it ships.
Especially useful for libraries where a compromised publish would matter
-- authentication, payments, cryptography, infrastructure -- but the
gates are valuable for any package.

If you want your CI to decide the version number for you,
semantic-release or release-please will serve you better.
This tool is for authors who want to make that call themselves
(or use the auto-release.yml companion for zero-dep commit-driven automation).

## Quick start (reusable workflow)

Five-line caller workflow in your library's `.github/workflows/release.yml`:

```yaml
name: release
on:
  release:
    types: [published]
permissions:
  contents: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  release:
    uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/release.yml@v0
```

Then:

1. Configure npm trusted publishing on npmjs.com for YOUR repo and YOUR
   caller workflow file (not forgesworn/anvil). See "Trusted publisher
   setup" below.
2. Bump package.json version and add a CHANGELOG.md entry.
3. Commit, tag (v1.2.3), push, and create a GitHub Release for the tag.

Libraries with frozen test vectors can add a gate:

```yaml
    with:
      vector-test-command: npm run test:vectors
```

## Version strategies

### Manual (default)

You bump package.json, write the CHANGELOG entry, tag, and create a
GitHub Release. The action verifies the tag matches and runs all gates.

### Verify

You still bump manually, but the action parses conventional commits
and fails the release if your bump is smaller than what the commits
imply. A feat: commit with only a patch bump is caught.

```yaml
    with:
      version-strategy: verify
```

### Auto (companion workflow)

The auto-release.yml companion workflow replaces semantic-release
entirely. It runs on push to main, parses conventional commits,
determines the bump, updates package.json and CHANGELOG.md, tags,
and creates a GitHub Release -- which triggers the main release pipeline.

```yaml
name: auto-release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  auto-release:
    uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/auto-release.yml@v0
```

Keep your existing release.yml (the publish pipeline) alongside it.

Note: the default GITHUB_TOKEN can create releases but cannot trigger
further workflow runs. If you need the auto-created release to trigger
release.yml automatically, use a GitHub App token or PAT with
contents: write scope. Set this as a repo secret and reference it in
the caller workflow's `secrets: inherit` or pass it as a named secret.

## Architecture

The reusable workflow runs as a four-job DAG:

```
   build-a ──────┐
   (full gates +  │
    record)       ├──> reproduce ──> publish
   build-b ──────┘    (compare      (publish-npm,
   (build +           sha256s)       publish-jsr,
    record)                          update-release)
```

### build-a (all gates)

1. Checkout your repo and this action at the pinned SHA
2. Setup Node with OIDC registry configured
3. verify-action-pins -- scan workflows for unpinned uses: refs
4. npm ci
5. npm run build --if-present
6. verify-tag -- git tag matches package.json version
7. verify-bump -- (only with version-strategy: verify) checks commits
8. run-tests -- full test suite (npm test by default)
9. verify-vectors -- frozen-vector gate (skipped if not configured)
10. verify-audit -- npm audit --omit=dev (runtime deps only)
11. verify-exports -- every exports subpath exists on disk
12. verify-secrets -- grep dist/ and files paths for secret markers
13. record-tarball -- npm pack with normalised mtimes, hash, write meta

### build-b (parallel build)

Same checkout, setup, npm ci, build, record-tarball on a second runner.
No gates -- only build and pack.

### reproduce

Downloads both tarball metas and compares sha256s. Under strict mode
(default), a mismatch blocks the release. Under warn mode, it logs and
continues. Under off mode, build-b and reproduce are skipped entirely.

### publish

Downloads the canonical tarball from build-a and runs:
- publish-npm -- idempotent npm publish via OIDC
- publish-jsr -- only if jsr.json exists
- update-release -- CHANGELOG extraction, integrity block, asset upload

## Step scripts

All in steps/, all bash, all sourcing lib.sh for shared helpers:

| Script | Purpose |
|---|---|
| verify-tag.sh | Git tag matches package.json version |
| verify-bump.sh | Conventional commits match version bump (verify mode) |
| run-tests.sh | Full test suite |
| verify-vectors.sh | Frozen-vector gate |
| verify-audit.sh | npm audit --omit=dev |
| verify-exports.sh | Every exports subpath exists on disk |
| verify-secrets.sh | Secret scan over pack set |
| verify-action-pins.sh | Warn/fail on unpinned uses: in workflows |
| normalise-mtimes.sh | Touch all files to SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH |
| record-tarball.sh | npm pack, hash, write tarball.meta |
| compare-tarball-meta.sh | Reproducibility gate (compare two metas) |
| publish-npm.sh | Publish the exact recorded tarball via OIDC |
| publish-jsr.sh | JSR publish if jsr.json exists |
| update-release.sh | CHANGELOG extraction, integrity block, asset upload |
| changelog-extract.sh | Parse CHANGELOG.md for the version section |
| parse-commits.sh | Parse conventional commits for auto-release |
| lib.sh | Shared helpers (header, log, warn, die, require_cmds) |

## Inputs (reusable workflow)

| Input | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| node-version | 24.11.0 | Node version (must ship npm >= 11.5.x for OIDC) |
| registry-url | https://registry.npmjs.org | npm registry URL |
| test-command | npm test | Full test suite command |
| vector-test-command | (empty) | Frozen-vector gate command (skip if empty) |
| changelog-file | CHANGELOG.md | Path to changelog |
| package-json | package.json | Path to package.json |
| audit-level | low | npm audit threshold (low/moderate/high/critical) |
| version-strategy | manual | manual: you bump and tag; verify: also checks conventional commits |
| reproducibility-mode | strict | strict: block on mismatch; warn: log only; off: skip build-b |
| strict-action-pins | true | Fail on unpinned uses: refs in consumer workflows |
| dry-run | false | Skip real publish |
| debug | false | Diagnostic logging for OIDC issues |

Secrets:

| Secret | When needed |
|---|---|
| JSR_TOKEN | Only if jsr.json exists. JSR does not yet support OIDC. |

## Composite action (alternative)

For consumers who need custom job structure, the composite action
bypasses the reusable workflow:

```yaml
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: forgesworn/anvil@v0
        with:
          vector-test-command: npm run test:vectors
```

The composite action does NOT include the reproducible-build gate
(build-b and reproduce jobs). It accepts the same inputs as the
reusable workflow except reproducibility-mode.

## Trusted publisher setup

npm's trusted publisher matches against the OIDC token's workflow_ref
claim -- the caller workflow, not the reusable workflow.

Configure on npmjs.com -> your package -> Settings -> Trusted Publisher:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Publisher | GitHub Actions |
| Organization or user | your GitHub org/user |
| Repository | your package's repo (NOT forgesworn/anvil) |
| Workflow filename | your caller workflow file (e.g. release.yml) |
| Environment | (leave empty) |

For the first publish of a brand-new package, you may need to create the
package on npm first (npm publish --access public from a workstation with
a granular access token), then configure trusted publishing for all
subsequent releases.

## Reproducible builds (detailed)

The reusable workflow runs two independent builds in parallel on two
GitHub Actions runners. Both pack the artefact with normalised mtimes
and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH derived from git log -1 --format=%ct.

How it works:

1. record-tarball.sh derives SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from the git commit
2. normalise-mtimes.sh touches all files (excluding node_modules/.git)
   to that epoch
3. npm pack --json produces the tarball
4. sha256 computed via shasum -a 256
5. sha512 integrity extracted from npm pack --json output
6. tarball.meta written with filename, size, sha256, integrity

The reproduce job downloads both metas and compares sha256s. On match,
the GitHub Release body gains a "Reproducible build" badge. On
mismatch (strict mode), the release is blocked with both hashes printed
and a tar-listing diff showing which files drifted.

Common non-determinism sources: Date.now() in build output, sorted-by-fs
globs, random IDs in build scripts, host paths in source maps.

Limitations:
- Single OS only (ubuntu-24.04). Cross-OS is not in scope.
- Two-run sample size. Probabilistic non-determinism may not show.
- SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is opt-in for build tools. Belt-and-braces mtime
  normalisation closes the file-stamp gap but embedded timestamps in
  compiled output are the consumer's bug to fix.

## Exports-map check (detailed)

verify-exports.sh catches the "deleted src/foo.ts but forgot to update
exports" class of bug. Neither publint nor arethetypeswrong performs
this file-existence check.

What it validates:
- Modern exports field: walks the entire .exports tree via jq, including
  all conditional keys (import, require, types, node, browser, default),
  nested conditionals, and string shorthand
- Legacy entry points: main, module, types, typings, bin (both string
  and object forms)
- Deduplicates paths so each file is checked exactly once

No configuration required. Runs automatically in build-a. If any
exported path does not exist on disk, exit 1 and the release is blocked.

## Runtime-only npm audit (detailed)

verify-audit.sh runs npm audit --omit=dev so devDependency advisories
do not block releases. Only production dependencies (those in
"dependencies", not "devDependencies") are evaluated.

The audit-level input (default: low) controls the severity threshold.
For security-sensitive libraries, even low-severity runtime advisories
are worth investigating before publishing.

## Action-pin auditing (detailed)

verify-action-pins.sh walks .github/workflows/*.yml in your repo and
flags every uses: owner/repo@ref whose ref is not a 40-character hex
SHA. Motivated by the tj-actions/changed-files March 2025 incident.

Special cases:
- Local actions (./ paths): skipped
- forgesworn/anvil: self-exempt to avoid circular failure
- Docker references: checks for sha256: digest pinning

strict-action-pins (default: true) controls whether unpinned refs
block the release or only warn.

## Secret scan (detailed)

verify-secrets.sh scans the publish pack set (dist/ plus any paths in
package.json "files") for:
- Forbidden filenames: .env, id_rsa, *.pem, etc.
- Secret content patterns: PEM private key blocks, Nostr nsec1,
  AWS/GitHub/Slack tokens

Known limitations:
- Content scans skip .md/.txt/.rst/.adoc files (crypto libraries
  legitimately include example secret-shaped strings in docs)
- Scan roots come from package.json "files" plus dist/. Libraries
  without explicit "files" may have a scan gap. Recommendation:
  always declare an explicit "files" array.

## Tarball integrity stamping

After all gates pass, the GitHub Release body is updated with:

```
## Artefact integrity

file:      my-package-1.2.0.tgz
size:      12345 bytes
sha256:    abc123...
sha512-base64...

Verify against the registry tarball:

curl -sLO https://registry.npmjs.org/my-package/-/my-package-1.2.0.tgz
shasum -a 256 my-package-1.2.0.tgz
```

The tarball is also uploaded as a GitHub Release asset. Consumers have
two independent sources for the bytes (npm + GitHub Releases).

On a clean re-run, publish-npm fetches the registry's dist.integrity
and compares to the local recorded value. Match = silent skip.
Mismatch = loud failure (registry tarball substitution alarm).

## CHANGELOG format

The extractor is intentionally loose. Matches the first heading (H1/H2/H3)
containing the version string and a dotted numeric pattern. Capture
continues until the next version heading. Works with Keep a Changelog
format and semantic-release's format.

## Troubleshooting

### OIDC token exchange error

If npm publish fails with "OIDC token exchange error - package not found",
the trusted publisher is configured for the wrong repo. Change the
Repository field on npmjs.com to your package's own repo.

If that doesn't fix it, add debug: true to your caller workflow and
re-run. The diagnostic step dumps npm version, redacted .npmrc, OIDC
env var presence, and npm config list.

### Reproducible build failure

Common causes printed in the failure message:
- Date.now() in build output (use a constant or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH)
- Glob order varying between runners (sort explicitly)
- Random IDs in build scripts (seed or remove)
- Host paths in source maps (use relative paths)

Set reproducibility-mode: warn to unblock while investigating.

### First publish of a new package

OIDC trusted publishing requires the package to already exist on npm.
For brand-new packages, do a one-time manual publish first:
npm publish --access public (with a granular access token), then
configure trusted publishing for subsequent releases.

## Threat model summary

Defends against:
- Compromised NPM_TOKEN (OIDC replaces long-lived tokens)
- Malicious release-tooling devDependencies (zero deps)
- Accidental publish of wrong version (verify-tag)
- Secrets in artefacts (verify-secrets)
- Broken frozen protocol outputs (verify-vectors)
- Exports/files drift (verify-exports)
- Runtime dep advisories (verify-audit)
- Tag-mutation supply-chain attacks (verify-action-pins)
- Non-deterministic builds masking regressions (reproduce gate)
- Registry tarball substitution (integrity comparison on re-run)

Does NOT defend against:
- Malicious maintainer
- Compromised GitHub
- Compromised npm registry
- Build-time exploit via consumer devDependencies

Full threat model: https://github.com/forgesworn/anvil/blob/main/THREAT-MODEL.md

## Comparison with alternatives

| | anvil | semantic-release | changesets | release-please | release-it | np |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dependencies | 0 | 28 direct | 26 direct | n/a | 23 direct | 36 direct |
| OIDC publishing | required | optional | no | no | optional | no |
| Reproducible builds | yes (two-runner) | no | no | no | no | no |
| Secret scan | yes | no | no | no | no | no |
| Exports check | yes | no | no | no | no | no |
| Monorepo | no | via plugins | native | yes | via plugins | no |
| Runtime | bash (CI) | Node.js | Node.js | TypeScript (CI) | Node.js | Node.js |

When NOT to use anvil:
- Monorepo -> use changesets
- Large plugin ecosystem needed -> use semantic-release
- Publish from laptop -> use np
- GitLab -> use release-it
- PR review gate before bumps -> use release-please

## Supported registries

| Registry | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| npm | supported | OIDC trusted publishing, provenance on every publish |
| JSR | supported | Opt-in via jsr.json, uses JSR_TOKEN (no OIDC yet) |
